prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B046 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 files show that all six of us reached it independently, but I do not rely on that count. The scientific case is the chain from proglucagon processing and human GLP-1 secretion and insulinotropic action, through the identification of the biologically active truncated peptide, to randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. It has been confirmed independently for decades, and the clinical effect is already large, so maturity is not in doubt. The citation names the physiology and the active form and mentions therapy only as the consequence. That keeps the prize on discovery and does not tie it to any one product. The chair's questions did not change my view of the science. They sharpened my view of the credit. Because B046 is mature and complete, I see no reason to give up a B046 name for a second part.
statement.case_against: The credit is still the weak point and I cannot settle it from the evidence supplied. Mojsov's priority on GLP-1(7-36) is contested and Habener is outside the credited names. Knudsen, who led the design of liraglutide and semaglutide, is not in my trio, so a physiology-centred prize will be read as leaving out the people who made the drugs durable. I accept that cost, but I also think the committee must say so openly. If the committee decides the achievement is the drugs, my trio is wrong and Knudsen would have to be weighed against Drucker or Holst. I would then want the citation rewritten around the therapies. A second part would also cost a B046 name under the three-person cap. The strongest second achievement, CAR-T (B028), has the Eshhar problem, which weakens any two- or three-name credit, and I think that problem is larger than my round-1 statement allowed.

responses.point: The chair moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov in round 1, while still saying that Knudsen's durable long-acting analogues were a genuine scientific achievement and not mere engineering.
responses.response: I accept your correction. Calling Knudsen's work engineering understated it, since making a peptide with a short half-life into a once-weekly drug with outcome benefit took real science. My reason for keeping Mojsov is narrower. This prize is meant to honour the discovery that made the therapy conceivable, and the active peptide is a necessary link in that chain. I share your answer to your own question on priority. The supplied record does not let me decide between Mojsov and Habener, and I think dropping a credited name on an unverified dispute would be the less defensible choice. I would change my position only if the committee chose a development-centred citation, and I would then expect Knudsen to displace Mojsov, not Drucker or Holst.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would cite the physiological discovery and name the peptide chemistry modestly, and prefers that to omitting Mojsov on an unverified claim. She also keeps CAR-T as her clear second choice and would pair it with GLP-1 only if the committee wants two parts.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and have kept wording close to yours: the physiology and the active form, with the therapies as consequence. On pairing, I would not accept a second part, because the cap would take a name from B046, and the only way to fit CAR-T is a two-person B028, which leaves Eshhar out. That would be a worse credit than the GLP-1 one. Your point on long-term safety does not alter my view of timing or wording. It is a matter of continuing data in a mature field, and the citation does not claim anything about the long-term safety of obesity indications.

responses.point: Sandberg objected to including Rosenberg in B028 because adoptive cell transfer and TIL work are a different achievement from the engineered receptor. He also argued that the missing Eshhar origin is a larger problem than I had allowed.
responses.response: Having reread your argument alongside Perlmann's, I agree with you on both points. Rosenberg's contribution to adoptive cell transfer is real, but it is not the CAR design, and a three-name CAR-T credit that includes him and excludes Eshhar does not describe the discovery cleanly. I would now support only June and Sadelain if B028 were ever built, and I would still flag Eshhar. That lowers B028 as an alternative for me, though I keep it as the next candidate because it has approved products and durable remissions. I still rank B007 below it on breadth. We have not tested that difference, because neither of us is proposing either one as a prize part. Separately, we have co-authored other work, which I record in my conflict note.

responses.point: Perlmann keeps Mojsov over Knudsen and says a contested priority must be resolved on the documentary record and not by leaving her off. He also says the attribution problem with CAR-T is worse than that with GLP-1.
responses.response: On both points I agree with you. A priority dispute does not remove a contribution. Without a documentary check we would be settling it by exclusion, which is the same arbitrary result in the other direction. I do not read the record as showing Mojsov's contribution to be weaker than Holst's or Drucker's. Your remark about CAR-T has moved me. In round 1 I treated Eshhar as a gap that could be noted. I now treat it as a real obstacle to calling any credited set the originators. I still list B028 as an alternative, but only as the strongest of the second-tier options, and I would not defend it ahead of B046 under the same attribution test.

responses.point: El Manira agrees with the Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann set for optogenetics, but says it is a tool and not a disease mechanism, and would not let it displace B046 in a single-achievement prize.
responses.response: We agree. I keep B038 as an alternative only because the methodological impact is exceptional and independently confirmed, not because I would set it against GLP-1. Reducing six credited names to three would leave out Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, and that makes it a poor candidate for this year. In a single-part prize I would not set it against B046. The shared point is the one you made: a tool prize should be weighed against a candidate with both mechanism and clinical outcome, and this year B046 is that candidate.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority on the active GLP-1(7-36) form holds against the primary record, and whether Habener's omission from the credited names will be read as unjust.
Whether the committee decides the achievement is the physiology or the drugs. In the second case my trio is wrong and Knudsen would need to be weighed against Drucker or Holst.
Whether a CAR-T credit to June and Sadelain can be defended with Eshhar outside the credited names, and whether the six-way optogenetics credit can be reduced to three.
I cannot judge from the supplied text how the wider scientific community or the public will read a single-part prize that excludes the drug developers.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal ground for any shortlisted ballot. My research (single-cell genomics, brain atlases, spatial transcriptomics) does not involve the credited names on B046, B028, B038, B011, B029, B007, B019 or B050, and my profile records no co-authorship or institutional tie to them. Sandberg's round-1 file records co-authorship with me on other work. It is committee-internal and involves no credited name, so I disclose it for transparency and not as a recusal ground. There is no change since round 1.
